You won't know who I am unless you've read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn't matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote it, and most of what he said was true. He exaggerated a few things, but mostly he told the truth. That's nothing unusual. I've never met anyone who didn't lie now and then, except Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—that's Tom's Aunt Polly—and Mary and the Widow Douglas are all in that book, which is mostly true, with some exaggerations, like I already said.

Here's how the book ends: Tom and I discovered the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and we became rich. We each got six thousand dollars, every bit of it gold. It made an astonishing pile. Judge Thatcher took it and invested it for us, and the interest brought us a dollar each every day, all year long—more money than anyone could figure out how to spend. The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me. But being in the house all the time was hard, especially with the widow so drearily proper and orderly about everything. When I couldn't bear it anymore, I ran away. I put my old rags back on and moved into my big sugar barrel again, free and happy. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he was starting a gang of robbers. I could join if I returned to the widow and acted respectable. So back I went.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and plenty of other names too, though she meant no harm. She dressed me in those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and feel hemmed in. Then the old routine started over. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to be there on time. Once you sat down, you couldn't start eating; you had to wait while she lowered her head and muttered complaints over the food, though there wasn't really anything wrong with it. Nothing, that is, except that everything had been cooked separately. It's different with a barrel of scraps: everything mixes together, the juices mingle, and the food tastes better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers. I was desperate to hear all about him, but eventually she let slip that Moses had been dead for a very long time. After that I lost interest, because dead people don't mean anything to me.

Her position was indeed one of unusual difficulty and trial. Though she burned with eagerness to discover the secret surrounding Oliver's past, she felt bound to respect the trust which the unhappy woman she had just spoken with had placed in her as an innocent young girl. The woman's speech and bearing had moved Rose Maylie deeply; and alongside her love for the boy entrusted to her, scarcely less sincere or fervent, arose a tender desire to reclaim the outcast for penitence and hope.

Their intention was to stay in London for only three days before spending several weeks upon a distant stretch of coast. Already it was midnight on the first day. What plan could she devise and put into effect within forty-eight hours? How might she delay their departure without awakening suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them and would remain another two days; but Rose knew the good gentleman's impetuous nature too well. She could foresee too plainly the anger with which, at the first outburst of indignation, he would view the person instrumental in Oliver's recapture. She dared not confide in him while no experienced person was present to support her pleading for the girl. These same considerations called for extreme care and discretion in telling Mrs. Maylie, whose immediate impulse would certainly be to consult the worthy doctor. For the same cause, approaching a legal adviser was scarcely possible to contemplate, even had she known how to proceed. Once she thought of asking Harry for assistance; but this brought back their last farewell, and she felt it would be unworthy to summon him again when—as tears gathered at this reflection—he might already have learned to forget her and find greater happiness at a distance.

Troubled by these conflicting thoughts, leaning first towards one course, then another, and shrinking from them all as fresh objections arose, Rose spent an anxious, sleepless night. After further inward debate the following day, she reached the desperate resolution to consult Harry.

“If returning here causes him pain,” she reflected, “what pain it will cause me! But perhaps he will not come. He might write instead, or come in person and carefully avoid seeing me, as he did before he left. I hardly expected that of him; yet it was better for both of us.” At this point Rose let fall her pen and turned aside, as if even the sheet of paper intended to carry her message must not witness her tears.

The group split between two neighbouring benches. Anne sat with those in front, and Mr Elliot, helped by his friend Colonel Wallis, had arranged things so successfully that he secured the place beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and receiving most of Colonel Wallis's courteous attentions, was perfectly satisfied.

Anne was in just the right frame of mind to enjoy the evening's entertainment: it gave her exactly enough to occupy her. She could respond emotionally to the tender pieces, cheerfully to the lively ones, attentively to the technically demanding, and patiently to the tedious. She had never enjoyed a concert more, at least through its first act. Near the end of it, during the pause after an Italian song, she explained the lyrics to Mr Elliot. They shared a concert programme.

“That,” she said, “is roughly the sense of it—or rather, the meaning of the words, since one certainly cannot speak of sense in an Italian love song. It is as close to the meaning as I can manage, anyway. I don't claim to understand the language. My Italian is very poor.”

“Yes, yes, I can see that. Clearly you know nothing about it. You know only enough to translate these Italian lines, with their inverted phrases, rearranged words and shortened forms, at first sight into clear, understandable, elegant English. There is no need to say any more about your ignorance. Here is all the evidence we need.”

“I won't argue against such kind politeness, but I would hate to be tested by someone truly proficient.”

“I haven't had the pleasure of visiting Camden Place for so long,” he replied, “without learning something about Miss Anne Elliot. I consider her too modest for people in general to know even half her accomplishments, and so accomplished that modesty would be unnatural in any other woman.”

“For shame! Really, that is far too much flattery. I've forgotten what's coming next,” she said, turning to the programme.

“Perhaps,” Mr Elliot said quietly, “I have known about your character for longer than you realize.”

“Really? How? You can only have known me since I arrived in Bath, unless you had heard my family speak of me before.”

“I knew of you by reputation long before you came to Bath. People who knew you intimately had described you to me. I have known what you were like for years: your appearance, your temperament, your accomplishments, your manner. I was familiar with them all.”

Mr Elliot succeeded in arousing precisely the interest he had hoped for. No one can resist the attraction of a mystery like that.
